item.research_question: Can the magnetocaloric properties of fully transition metal-based high entropy alloys be tuned via FCC metal additives and heat treatment to achieve a second-order magnetic phase transition with improved refrigerant capacity?
item.processing_route: Arc furnace melting under argon atmosphere using 99.99% purity elements; cold rolled into sheets (100–250 μm); annealed for one hour at 900 °C in Ta foil wrapped quartz tubes with Ar gas; characterized in as-rolled and annealed states.
item.test_conditions: Magnetic measurements via Quantum Design PPMS with VSM option; M(H) loops from 0 to 50 kOe; isotherms from 10 K to 350 K in 5 K steps; Tc estimated at maximum dM/dT in 2 kOe field; XRD via θ–2θ with Cu Kα photons.
key_findings: Tc increases monotonically from approximately 100 K (0% Pd) to 280 K (11.11% Pd) in the annealed state.
Saturation magnetization (Ms) at 5 K increases from approximately 30 emu/g to 46 emu/g with Pd addition.
Refrigerant capacity (RC) is enhanced by nearly 40% in annealed samples with less than 1.5% Pd.
Universal scaling analysis shows a decrease in the homogeneity variance statistic (F) of at least 50% with annealing or Pd incorporation.
The entropy change exponent (n) decreases toward the mean field theory prediction (2/3) with Pd addition and annealing.
The refrigerant capacity exponent (m) becomes superlinear (e.g., 1.13 for annealed 5.88% Pd) compared to the unannealed x=0 sample (0.99).
As-rolled samples show an artificial ~25% higher RC than annealed samples due to disorder broadening the exchange parameter distribution.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that Pd additions and heat treatment reduce structural defects (strain, vacancies, stacking faults) and grain size reduction, leading to a reduction in the distribution of exchange energies. This homogenization of the alloy results in a more magnetically homogeneous system that exhibits behavior closer to mean field theory and a 'carat' shaped magnetic entropy change curve.
item.limitations: The maximum entropy change is about a factor of 20 less than Gadolinium (Gd), and the Pd-containing alloy is ten times as expensive as Gd. The authors also note that the broadening of the entropy peak in as-rolled samples leads to an artificially enhanced refrigerant capacity that may not reflect intrinsic material performance.
item.future_work: The authors propose investigating other FCC metals like Cu or Ag to tune magnetism with significantly reduced material costs. They also suggest that computational materials scientists can survey the large parameter space of these alloys due to their observed mean field behavior, and recommend high-resolution neutron scattering to probe bulk structural information.
quotes: heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy.
RC is enhanced with Pd by nearly 50% and 60% in the as-rolled and annealed samples, respectively.
The F statistic was calculated only for the values of θ > 0 in order to compare all samples with the same protocol

Question: Can the magnetocaloric properties of fully transition metal-based high entropy alloys be tuned via FCC metal additives and heat treatment to achieve a second-order magnetic phase transition with improved refrigerant capacity?. System: Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx (x = 0.00% to 11.11% atomic Pd). Processing: Arc furnace melting under argon atmosphere using 99.99% purity elements; cold rolled into sheets (100–250 μm); annealed for one hour at 900 °C in Ta foil wrapped quartz tubes with Ar gas; characterized in as-rolled and annealed states.. Test conditions: Magnetic measurements via Quantum Design PPMS with VSM option; M(H) loops from 0 to 50 kOe; isotherms from 10 K to 350 K in 5 K steps; Tc estimated at maximum dM/dT in 2 kOe field; XRD via θ–2θ with Cu Kα photons.. Findings: Tc increases monotonically from approximately 100 K (0% Pd) to 280 K (11.11% Pd) in the annealed state.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) at 5 K increases from approximately 30 emu/g to 46 emu/g with Pd addition.; Refrigerant capacity (RC) is enhanced by nearly 40% in annealed samples with less than 1.5% Pd.; Universal scaling analysis shows a decrease in the homogeneity variance statistic (F) of at least 50% with annealing or Pd incorporation.; The entropy change exponent (n) decreases toward the mean field theory prediction (2/3) with Pd addition and annealing.; The refrigerant capacity exponent (m) becomes superlinear (e.g., 1.13 for annealed 5.88% Pd) compared to the unannealed x=0 sample (0.99).; As-rolled samples show an artificial ~25% higher RC than annealed samples due to disorder broadening the exchange parameter distribution.. Mechanism: The authors argue that Pd additions and heat treatment reduce structural defects (strain, vacancies, stacking faults) and grain size reduction, leading to a reduction in the distribution of exchange energies. This homogenization of the alloy results in a more magnetically homogeneous system that exhibits behavior closer to mean field theory and a 'carat' shaped magnetic entropy change curve.. Limitations: The maximum entropy change is about a factor of 20 less than Gadolinium (Gd), and the Pd-containing alloy is ten times as expensive as Gd. The authors also note that the broadening of the entropy peak in as-rolled samples leads to an artificially enhanced refrigerant capacity that may not reflect intrinsic material performance.. Future work: The authors propose investigating other FCC metals like Cu or Ag to tune magnetism with significantly reduced material costs. They also suggest that computational materials scientists can survey the large parameter space of these alloys due to their observed mean field behavior, and recommend high-resolution neutron scattering to probe bulk structural information..
